solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Double served with beer for Glastonbury star

explanation.surface: A festival-goer orders a double with a pint while watching the headliner.
explanation.walkthrough: Glastonbury is England's biggest music festival, which this pop singer headlined. The enumeration (3,4) hides where the double ends and the beer begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Dua Lipa is a pop singer who has topped the bill at Glastonbury.

clue.text: Leaving university begin something outstanding

explanation.surface: A graduate leaves university to start a brilliant career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise, but here it means unpaid — a debt is money still outstanding. Remove U from DEBUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt is an amount still outstanding, i.e. owed.

clue.text: Circus performer in dress almost grabbed by a lion?

indicators.note: the last letter of ROBE is dropped
To be grabbed by someone is to be held in their clutches.

parts.note: a lion is, for example, a cat; ROB goes after the C

explanation.surface: A circus act where a performer in costume is seized by the big cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a lion is only an example of a cat: A C(ROB)AT.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrobats, tumbling and flying on the trapeze, are a staple of the big top: a plain synonym by category.

clue.text: One story's no good about designated victim

parts.note: a saga is a long story; SAGA's = SAGA has
G = good, removed from SAGA to leave SAA

explanation.surface: A crime novel with a nasty plot about a marked victim.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Abraham was told to sacrifice his son Isaac, who was spared at the last moment — so Isaac was designated as the victim.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac was the son God told Abraham to offer as a sacrifice.

clue.text: Basil for example a sentimental sort missing the point

definitions.note: AROMATIC is used as a noun here: a fragrant plant.

indicators.note: Something missing is absent.

parts.note: N = north, a point of the compass; removed

explanation.surface: Basil — a man's name — is described as a soppy type lacking sharpness.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil reads as a man's name, which suits 'a sentimental sort'; it is the herb. 'The point' is a compass point, here N.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: basil is one of the aromatics, the fragrant herbs cooks use, taking AROMATIC as a noun.

clue.text: Came around, receiving ball on right side, finding Shearer?

indicators.note: To come around is to turn back on yourself.
the right-hand end of 'ball', its last letter

parts.note: the letter at the right-hand end of BALL

explanation.surface: A footballer comes round and gets the ball on the right wing, looking for Alan Shearer.
explanation.walkthrough: Shearer suggests Alan Shearer the England striker, fitting the football surface; here it is someone who shears. DELI(L)AH.
explanation.definitionFit: Delilah cut off Samson's hair, taking his strength — a shearer in the Bible.

clue.text: Stone set in ring farthest from centre

parts.note: to ring = to dial a phone; ST goes after DI
st = stone, the unit of weight

explanation.surface: A jeweller sets a stone in a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set in ring' makes you think of jewellery; the stone is the weight abbreviation and the ring is a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: Distal is the anatomical term for the part farthest from the body's centre.

clue.text: Drop proceedings in which I would never appear?

definitions.text: in which I would never appear?
definitions.note: The definition is a description of LOWER CASE rather than a synonym.

explanation.surface: A witness hopes to drop a lawsuit they want no part of.
explanation.walkthrough: The pronoun I is always written as a capital, so it never appears in lower case.
explanation.definitionFit: Lower case is the small letters, and the pronoun I is always a capital.

clue.text: One always behind Labour lass on the rise

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read upwards

parts.note: a drag = a labour, a tiresome task

explanation.surface: A political picture: someone always trailing the Labour party's rising young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour with a capital looks like the political party; it is plain toil. DRAG GAL is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard is someone who always falls behind.

clue.text: Conservative sporting dodgy hairstyle wildly funny

indicators.note: HAIRSTYLE is unreliable, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Tory MP with a ridiculous haircut is a laughing stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wildly' looks like a second anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hysterical is used informally to mean extremely funny.

clue.text: Wild fire appearing shortly after wounding remark

indicators.note: 'After' means following in order.

parts.note: to fire (up) = to arouse; cut to AROUS

explanation.surface: A spiteful comment soon sparks a furious outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the pieces back to front: 'appearing after' puts the fire behind the remark, so read the wordplay's second half first.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbarous means savage, uncivilised — wild.

clue.text: Seam rolled back to cover silver screw

definitions.note: Screw is singular slang; WAGES is plural in form but names the same single pay packet.

indicators.note: A thing rolled back turns over on itself.
To cover is to wrap round, so the reversed seam goes around the silver.

parts.note: to seam = to sew; reversed to WES, AG goes after W
Ag, the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A tailor turns back a seam over a silver screw.
explanation.walkthrough: Screw is British slang for wages, pay. The surface makes it a piece of hardware.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, a screw is someone's wage or salary.

clue.text: Sneak exiting card game left with golden award

indicators.note: Something exiting leaves the room, so the sneak's letters walk out of the card game.

parts.note: the casino game; minus RAT leaves BACCA
a rat = a sneak, an informer

explanation.surface: A cheat slips out of the card room clutching a gold prize.
explanation.walkthrough: AUREATE is a rare literary word for golden. The baccalaureate is the French school-leaving qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: A baccalaureate is an academic qualification awarded on completing studies.

clue.text: Winning with Neath or Garryowen?

explanation.surface: A rugby match: the Welsh club Neath or the Irish club Garryowen scoring a win.
explanation.walkthrough: Neath and Garryowen look like two rugby clubs; Neath is really 'neath, under. A Garryowen, named after the Limerick club, is a high rugby kick chased by the kicker's team.
explanation.definitionFit: An up-and-under is another name for the Garryowen, a high kick in rugby.

clue.text: Poor film about a crime where folio goes astray

indicators.note: 'About' in its sense of around: the film wraps round the crime.

parts.note: a pic = a picture, a film; ATHET goes after the P
f = folio; removed to leave ATHET

explanation.surface: A critic pans a heist movie with a missing manuscript at its heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The film is PIC, the crime is A THEFT, and folio is the abbreviation F: P(A THE[F]T)IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic means miserably inadequate — poor.

clue.text: Other son securing flat for timely break

parts.note: else = other; EVEN goes after EL

explanation.surface: Another son holds onto a flat to take a well-timed break.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack and tea break, taken at around eleven o'clock — hence 'timely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a break named after the hour it is taken.

clue.text: Limits to growth set by India's Indira?

indicators.note: I is placed beside the rest

parts.note: the limits of GROWTH are G and H, spelt out as G AND H

indicators.note: the first and last letters of 'growth'

parts.note: India is I in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: India's prime minister Indira sets limits on the country's growth.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to spell out the limits literally: G AND H. 'India's' then supplies I, the phonetic-alphabet letter, and Indira is the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Indira Gandhi was prime minister of India; the question mark shows she is one example of a Gandhi.

clue.text: This writer against himself for the moment?

definitions.note: The definition is a phrase meaning 'in the meantime'; MEANTIME is the noun it contains.

parts.note: himself, i.e. the same writer, again ME

explanation.surface: A writer in two minds, arguing with himself for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Himself' refers back to 'this writer', so it gives ME a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: For the moment means in the meantime, the interval before something else happens.

clue.text: Saboteur losing heart becomes more virtuous

indicators.note: one of the two central Bs is dropped

parts.note: a nobbler tampers with racehorses; minus a middle B

explanation.surface: A saboteur loses his nerve and turns good.
explanation.walkthrough: To nobble is British slang for sabotaging a racehorse or bribing a juror, so a nobbler is a saboteur.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobler means of finer moral character — more virtuous.

clue.text: Danger lurks in Lizzy being cut near ribs

indicators.note: To lurk in a place is to hide inside it, so the danger hides within Lizzy's pet name.

parts.note: Bet, a pet form of Elizabeth like Lizzy; RISK goes after B

explanation.surface: A menacing warning that Lizzy is in danger of a knife near her ribs.
explanation.walkthrough: Lizzy and Bet are both short for Elizabeth, so one pet name stands for the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisket is a cut of beef from the breast, next to the ribs.

clue.text: Cook made to keep back especially grand rum

indicators.note: MADE is cooked, i.e. its letters are rearranged
To keep something is to hold it, so the cooked letters hold the grand word inside them.
'Back' means backwards, so the especially grand word is written in reverse.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters; ERAR goes after DEM

explanation.surface: A chef keeps back an especially grand rum for the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like the chef but is the anagram signal; DEM(ERAR)A. Demerara is a dark rum from Guyana, and also a brown sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara rum is distilled in Guyana, named after the Demerara river.

clue.text: Dancing-girl with special talent announced for calendar

parts.note: an alma (or almah) is an Egyptian dancing-girl

indicators.note: KNACK is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a knack is a special talent; said out, it gives NAC

explanation.surface: A showgirl with a special talent has her act listed in a calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: ALMA is a crossword stalwart: an Egyptian dancing-girl.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is an annual calendar with dates and information.

clue.text: Shrew at Padua carried by ship moves across ice

parts.note: SS = steamship; KATE goes after the first S
Kate is the shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, set in Padua

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean heroine carried by ship glides across the ice.
explanation.walkthrough: The shrew is Katherina (Kate) from The Taming of the Shrew, set in Padua.
explanation.definitionFit: To skate is to glide across ice on blades.

clue.text: Land in one piece meeting Benedictine?

parts.note: the king is a chess piece
Dom is the title of a Benedictine monk

explanation.surface: A monk arrives in the country safe and sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In one piece' looks like one phrase meaning intact; it splits into 'in one' and 'piece', a chessman. Dom is the title given to Benedictine monks.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the whole country of Britain and Northern Ireland is the land meant.

clue.text: Unusual wheels beneath extremely durable object

parts.note: the first and last letters of DURABLE

indicators.note: the outer letters of 'durable'

explanation.surface: A strange set of wheels under a very tough item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a noun, a thing, but is the verb: to object is to demur. Rum is British for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Here 'object' is the verb, to protest; demurring is voicing a mild objection.

clue.text: Italian agreement reversed by the French — in Ireland?

definitions.note: The definition is a cryptic pointer: Ireland is an example of an ISLE.

indicators.note: Reversed means turned the other way, so the Italian yes is written backwards.

explanation.surface: A European treaty between Italy and France, somehow concerning Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Ireland is an island, so an isle is what Ireland is 'in' — the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by the question mark: Ireland is an island, so the whole place is 'in' an isle.

clue.text: William and Harry say they're up for a fight?

definitions.meaning: William and Harry are royal princes, each given a ducal title on marrying
slang for fists, which go up before a fight

explanation.surface: The two princes are spoiling for a scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: Dukes is slang for fists, perhaps from rhyming slang Duke of Yorks = forks = hands; William and Harry are the Dukes of Cambridge and of Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: William and Harry are royal dukes; dukes are also fists.

clue.text: Accompaniments for dish: order smells terrible!

parts.note: trim = order, as in 'in good trim'
to ming is British slang for to stink

explanation.surface: A diner complains that the side dishes served with the meal stink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ming' is British slang for a bad smell. The trimmings are the traditional extras with a roast, such as stuffing and gravy.
explanation.definitionFit: Trimmings are the side dishes that accompany a main dish.

clue.text: Runs in Paris and is second — tries again?

indicators.note: 'and' and 'is' are put into French

explanation.surface: A runner in Paris comes second and wonders about another go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' applies to both 'and' and 'is'. The question mark admits that retesting is only loosely trying again.
explanation.definitionFit: To retest is to test again, and to try can mean to test.

clue.text: Each woman endlessly causes pain

parts.note: any woman's name will do; minus L gives RACHE

explanation.surface: Every woman who goes on and on is a pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' looks like it modifies 'causes'; it trims the woman's name. An earache is also British slang for being nagged.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym narrowed: an ache in the ear is one kind of pain, and the surface's nagging woman adds the slang sense.
